Lazarus was consumed by sores and death, but it happened that he was carried away by angels to Abraham's bosom; the rich man, however, who was excessively surrounded by wealth and flatteries, and was considered enviable and blessed, and often named as such, was handed over to the laws of nature and was swallowed up by the darkness of death; instead of earthly goods, he was exchanged for the judgment of Hades, paying the penalty of love of wealth; perhaps some of the listeners would say that if poverty has the boast of piety towards God and is valued by the law of righteousness, and has chosen the bitter vote for itself, how can this be; it is necessary to consider that wealth is often accompanied by many inappropriate things, and the rich are more prone to haughtiness and excess, while the poor are troubled and distressed, seeking to acquire something and find a moderate consolation for their needs

Besides all these things, I think it is necessary to say that each person's manner shapes the nature of their actions, according to their will, either to be counted among the vile or the admired; and whatever someone might say about the beauty from dyes, the same applies to the nature of things, according to the manner of the one who has them in hand; thus, the one who manages poverty wisely, being the best of all, I will say without hesitation; for if someone is content with little and has acquired the most necessary things with sweat, they offer prayers of thanksgiving; how could they not be worthy of praise, having a counselor for humility and having highly valued the law of self-control, so as to completely reject evil-doers? But the one who is conspicuous for their abundance of wealth, how could they not be justified, if they have a gracious God, by taking care of others and giving a little to those in need, and overcoming and enduring some kind of unrelenting misfortune, having made temporary wealth a servant of their own pleasure? Therefore, the poor man was in unexpected luxuries; the rich man, on the other hand, was unusually in fire and torments.

For if someone were to approach him at that opportune moment and speak to him, and were to ask to see how many possessions he might wish to sell in order to escape punishment, having chosen the better option, would he not readily agree to give up all his property for this? And what is uncertain about this? It is foolish and ignorant to think that one can learn through experience to endure terrible things, and that this is possible for those who wish to have it outside of necessity and compulsion. And if our worship is better than that of the Jews, how is it not clear to everyone that one should not think it necessary to conquer the excellence of the latter? The Savior himself told us this. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. What then did the law given through Moses, which was a type and shadow, teach those in Jerusalem to honor the equality of brothers? They, having despised the great and abundant manna, and having become hungry, were about to mourn the death of the all-wise Moses, and were saying that they could no longer be saved due to the overwhelming famine, and were already lamenting their funeral dirge. And having lost all hope, they were saying: Would that we had died, struck down in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots and ate bread to the full.

You led us into this wilderness to kill the whole congregation with hunger. Moses, being very wise, did not know what to do or say. But they, having hope only in God, showed the end of their expectation without hesitation. The Lord said to him, 'Behold, I will rain bread from heaven, and the people will go out and gather the daily portion.' Moses, interpreting the power of the law to the Israelites, said, 'This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat.' The word that the Lord commanded was to gather from it, each one according to the number of people, and to collect it in their tents. They did so, and the one who gathered much did not have more, and the one who gathered little did not have less. The Lord of the law did not allow gathering more than needed, only what was sufficient for today's food. If someone gathered more, the excess was turned into a swarm of worms, showing that the possession of what is sufficient is pleasant and blameless, but what is stored up uselessly and beyond need is the cause of worms.

What is the Savior to us? Make friends for yourselves from unjust wealth, so that when you fail, they will receive you into their tents. The Savior's power will be shown, and I will say something again. It is not possible to doubt that a moderate multitude of virtuous and gentle people does not escape God's notice. When we accept earthly goods as shared with others, no one should doubt that we will also share in the reward of gentleness. They will receive you into their tents, as it is written. The blessed Paul also understands this and says: Your abundance for their need, and their abundance for your need. Let us be kind to each other, compassionate, forgiving each other, just as God forgave us in Christ. What has God given us in Christ, or what good things have we been given to share? It is necessary to see. We have been given forgiveness of sins, unfailing love. We have been saved, having received forgetfulness, as it were, of God's human small-mindedness. Therefore, we must strive to follow the calmness that is in God, the Master of all, and to forgive, beloved. And we must wisely consider that there are countless human failures, and no one can be free from our small-mindedness.

But if we were to grieve over each of the accustomed things, we would be greatly distressed, and our whole life would be in bitterness and sorrows. And since the ways of the forgetful lead to death, as it is written, nothing prevents each soul from becoming a holder of death, because it cannot nobly cry out against the pain, always being provoked to fiercely resist the things that have happened. Therefore, as the blessed Paul said, let us bear each other's burdens. And in this way, we will fulfill the law of Christ. For this manner of piety is transparent. But there are some among us who are so far from wanting to be good, and they consider the boast of their own soul's forgetfulness as the greatest, so that even if some of those called to brotherhood stumble slightly, they, having condemned all, and having lifted up the entire linen like a sail, are carried away by uncontrollable impulses, and they trample like a bull, thinking that the opinion of not doing anything bad is most shameful, unless they do every terrible thing. But if some of those who have stumbled against them are stronger, many servants of savagery immediately surround them
pass_b_english: Lazarus, who was consumed by sores and death, was carried away by angels to Abraham's bosom.

In contrast, the rich man, who was excessively surrounded by wealth and flatteries, and was considered enviable and blessed, and his years were often regarded as superior, was handed over to the laws of nature and was swallowed up by the darkness of death.
Instead of earthly goods, he was exchanged for the judgment of Hades, paying the penalty of love of wealth.
This raises the question of how poverty, which has the boast of piety towards God and is valued by the law of righteousness, and has chosen the bitter vote for itself, can be considered a blessing.
Perhaps some would say that if poverty has chosen the bitter vote for itself, how can this be?

It is necessary to consider that wealth is often accompanied by many inappropriate things, and the rich are more prone to haughtiness and excess, while the poor are troubled and distressed, seeking to acquire something and find a moderate consolation for their needs.
In addition to all these things, it is necessary to consider how each person's manner influences the nature of their actions, shaping them according to their will, either for good or for ill.
Just as the beauty of an object can be enhanced by the application of dyes, so too can the nature of things be transformed by the manner in which they are handled.
The person who manages poverty wisely, for example, is truly the best of all, and I will say so without hesitation.
For if someone is content with little and has acquired the most necessary things through their own efforts, they offer prayers of thanksgiving.
How could they not be worthy of praise, having chosen a path of humility and self-control, and having rejected the ways of evil?

On the other hand, the person who is conspicuous for their abundance of wealth, and yet uses it to care for others and to alleviate the suffering of those in need, is truly justified in the eyes of God.
By overcoming and enduring the challenges of life, and by making temporary wealth a servant of their own pleasure, they demonstrate a profound understanding of what is truly important.

The story of the rich man and Lazarus comes to mind, where the poor man is rewarded with unexpected luxuries; the rich man, on the other hand, is punished with fire and torments, and his years, which were often named as better, are now filled with suffering.

If someone were to approach him at the most opportune moment and speak to him, asking to see how many possessions he might wish to sell in order to escape punishment, having chosen the better option, would he not readily agree to give up all his property for this?
It is foolish and ignorant to think that one can learn through experience to endure terrible things, and that this is possible for those who wish to have it outside of necessity and compulsion.
The Savior himself told us that unless our righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, we will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:20).
What then did the law given through Moses, which was a type and shadow, teach those in Jerusalem to honor the equality of brothers?

They, having despised the great and abundant manna, and having become hungry, were about to mourn the death of the all-wise Moses, and were saying that they could no longer be saved due to the overwhelming famine, and were already lamenting their funeral dirge, saying: 'Would that we had died, struck down in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots and ate bread to the full' (Exodus 16:3).
Moses, being very wise, did not know what to do or say.
But they, having hope only in God, showed the end of their expectation without hesitation.
The Lord then spoke to Moses, saying, 'Behold, I will provide bread from heaven, and the people will go out and gather their daily portion' (Exodus 16:4).

Moses interpreted the power of the law to the Israelites, explaining that this bread was a gift from the Lord, and that they should gather it, each one according to the number of people in their household, and collect it in their tents.
They did so, and surprisingly, the one who gathered much did not have more, and the one who gathered little did not have less.
This was because the Lord of the law did not allow them to gather more than they needed, only what was sufficient for that day's food.
If someone gathered more, the excess would be infested with worms, demonstrating that having just enough is pleasant and blameless, but storing up more than needed is a cause for worms.
The Savior teaches us to make friends for ourselves from unjust wealth, so that when we fail, they will receive us into their community.

The blessed Paul also understands this principle and applies it to the community of believers, saying that our abundance should be used to meet the needs of others, and their abundance should be used to meet our needs (2 Corinthians 8:14).
Let us be kind to each other, compassionate, forgiving each other, just as God forgave us in Christ.
We have been given forgiveness of sins and unfailing love, and we must strive to follow the calmness that is in God, the Master of all, and to forgive others, just as we have been forgiven.
This is not an easy task, as we are all prone to small-mindedness and failures, but it is necessary for us to grow in love and kindness.
If we were to grieve over every ordinary thing that happens, we would be deeply distressed, and our entire life would be filled with bitterness and sorrow.
Our lives would be marked by constant pain and sadness, and we would struggle to find any joy or peace.
The paths of those who are forgetful and vengeful lead to death, as it is written (Proverbs 12:28).
Nothing can stop each person's soul from being consumed by death, because they are unable to cry out against the pain in a noble way.
Instead, they are always being provoked to fiercely resist the things that have happened, and they are carried away by their emotions.
As the blessed Paul said, we should bear each other's burdens, and in this way, we will fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2).
This approach to piety is transparent and clear, and it is the key to living a life that is pleasing to God.
However, there are some people among us who are far from wanting to be good, and they take pride in their own soul's forgetfulness.
They consider it a great accomplishment to be able to forget the wrongs that have been done to them, and they look down on those who are not able to do the same.
If someone who is called to brotherhood stumbles slightly, they will condemn them completely, and they will be carried away by their uncontrollable impulses.
They will trample on others like a bull, thinking that the opinion of not doing anything bad is the most shameful thing.
They believe that unless they do every terrible thing, they are not truly living.
But if someone who has stumbled against them is stronger, they will be surrounded by many servants of savagery, and they will be in grave danger.
